1. Meaning of Rule of Law

Rule of Law means:

  • Law is supreme.
  • Every person and public authority is subject to law.
  • No individual, institution or Government is above the law.

Public power must be exercised:

  • According to law.
  • Within constitutional limits.
  • Without arbitrariness.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rule of Law → Supremacy of Law + Absence of Arbitrary Power

2. Rule of Law vs Rule of Men

Rule of Law:

  • Government according to law.
  • Legal limits on Government power.
  • Equality before law.
  • Judicial protection available.
  • Constitutional Government.

Rule of Men:

  • Government according to personal will.
  • Possibility of arbitrary power.
  • Unequal treatment.
  • Decisions depend on individual rulers.

3. Importance of Rule of Law

Rule of Law forms the foundation of:

  • Constitutional Government.
  • Democracy.
  • Justice.
  • Equality.
  • Good Governance.
  • Protection of liberty.
  • Accountability of Government.

4. Government Action Must Have Legal Authority

Every Government action must have:

  • Constitutional authority.
  • Statutory authority.
  • Other lawful legal basis.

Government cannot exercise power merely because:

  • It considers an action desirable.
  • An official personally prefers it.

5. Protection against Arbitrary Power

Rule of Law prohibits:

  • Arbitrary arrest.
  • Arbitrary detention.
  • Arbitrary deprivation of rights.
  • Arbitrary administrative decisions.
  • Unlawful discrimination.
  • Exercise of unrestricted Government discretion.

6. Origin of Modern Rule of Law

The modern systematic exposition of Rule of Law is associated with:

  • A.V. Dicey.
📌 Must-Memorise

A.V. Dicey → Rule of Law

7. A.V. Dicey's Famous Work

A.V. Dicey explained Rule of Law in:

  • Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution.

Published in:

  • 1885.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dicey → 1885

8. Dicey's Three Principles

A.V. Dicey identified:

  • Supremacy of Law.
  • Equality Before Law.
  • Predominance of Legal Spirit.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dicey → Supremacy + Equality + Legal Spirit

9. Supremacy of Law

The first Diceyan principle means:

  • No person may be punished except according to law.
  • No person may be arrested except according to law.
  • No person may be detained except according to law.
  • No rights may be taken away arbitrarily.
  • Government cannot exercise arbitrary authority.

10. Equality Before Law

The second Diceyan principle means:

  • Ordinary citizen and public official are subject to law.
  • Official position alone does not create immunity from ordinary legal accountability.
  • Special privilege merely because of status is inconsistent with the general principle of equality.

11. Predominance of Legal Spirit

Dicey's third principle emphasises protection of rights through:

  • Independent Courts.
  • Judicial decisions.
  • Ordinary legal remedies.

12. Independent Judiciary and Dicey

Predominance of legal spirit requires:

  • Independent judges.
  • Accessible courts.
  • Effective remedies.
  • Protection of individual liberty.

13. Expression Not Expressly Used

The expression:

  • “Rule of Law”

is not expressly used as a defined phrase in the Constitution.

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Rule of Law → Constitutional Principle

But → Not Expressly Defined in a Single Article

16. Preamble and Rule of Law

The Preamble seeks to secure:

  • Justice.
  • Liberty.
  • Equality.
  • Dignity of the individual.

17. Democratic Republic

The Preamble declares India a:

  • Sovereign.
  • Socialist.
  • Secular.
  • Democratic.
  • Republic.

Rule of Law ensures these constitutional principles operate within legal limits rather than through arbitrary political power.

21. Article 14 and Arbitrariness

Article 14 prohibits:

  • Arbitrary State action.
  • Unreasonable discrimination.

Governmental decisions must be:

  • Fair.
  • Reasonable.
  • Non-discriminatory.
  • Based on law.

22. Equality Before Law — Origin

Equality Before Law is derived from:

  • British constitutional law.
  • A.V. Dicey's Rule of Law.

23. Equality Before Law — Nature

Equality Before Law is described as a:

  • Negative concept.

It means:

  • Absence of special legal privilege.
  • Equal subjection to ordinary law.

24. Equal Protection of Laws — Origin

Equal Protection of Laws is derived from:

  • Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution.

25. Equal Protection of Laws — Nature

Equal Protection of Laws is a:

  • Positive concept.

It means:

  • Similarly situated persons should receive similar treatment under similar circumstances.

26. Equality Before Law vs Equal Protection

Equality Before Law:

  • Negative concept.
  • British origin.
  • No special privileges.
  • Equal legal status.

Equal Protection of Laws:

  • Positive concept.
  • U.S. origin.
  • Similar treatment of similarly situated persons.
  • Permits reasonable classification.

27. Reasonable Classification

Article 14 does not prohibit:

  • All classification.

It prohibits:

  • Arbitrary classification.

28. First Test of Valid Classification

Classification must be based on:

  • Intelligible Differentia.

This means:

  • There must be a clear basis distinguishing one group from another.

29. Second Test of Valid Classification

The differentia must have:

  • Rational Nexus

with:

  • Object sought to be achieved by the law.
📌 Must-Memorise

Reasonable Classification → Intelligible Differentia + Rational Nexus

69. Meaning of Natural Justice

Natural Justice means:

  • Fundamental fairness in decision-making.

Protection against:

  • Bias.
  • Arbitrary action.
  • Unfair procedure.

70. Application of Natural Justice

Natural Justice may apply to:

  • Administrative authorities.
  • Quasi-judicial authorities.
  • Judicial proceedings where applicable.

71. Two Main Principles

The two basic principles are:

  • Nemo Judex in Causa Sua.
  • Audi Alteram Partem.
📌 Must-Memorise

Natural Justice → No Bias + Fair Hearing

72. Nemo Judex in Causa Sua

Meaning:

  • No one should be a judge in his or her own cause.

This is called:

  • Rule Against Bias.

73. Rule Against Bias

Decision-maker must:

  • Be impartial.
  • Avoid personal interest.
  • Avoid prejudice.
  • Approach matter fairly.

74. Audi Alteram Partem

Meaning:

  • Hear the Other Side.

75. Fair Hearing Requirements

An affected person should ordinarily receive:

  • Notice.
  • Opportunity to present the case.
  • Opportunity to be heard.

76. Administrative Fairness

Administrative authorities must act:

  • Lawfully.
  • Fairly.
  • Reasonably.
  • Transparently.
  • Without arbitrariness.
  • Without discrimination.

77. Relevant Considerations

Administrative decisions should be based upon:

  • Relevant facts.
  • Proper procedures.
  • Statutory purpose.
  • Public interest.

78. Fair Procedure

Fair procedure generally includes:

  • Notice before adverse action.
  • Opportunity to be heard.
  • Impartial decision-maker.
  • Reasoned decision where legally required.
  • Compliance with statutory procedure.

79. Judicial Protection against Administrative Action

Courts may review administrative action violating:

  • Constitution.
  • Law.
  • Fundamental Rights.
  • Principles of Natural Justice.

80. Meaning of Judicial Review

Judicial Review means power of courts to examine whether:

  • Legislative action.
  • Executive action.
  • Constitutional amendment within Basic Structure limits

complies with Constitution.

81. Constitutional Basis of Judicial Review

The attachment identifies provisions including:

  • Article 13.
  • Article 32.

  • Article 136.
  • Article 226.
  • Article 227.

82. Judicial Review as Basic Structure

The Supreme Court has recognised:

  • Judicial Review

as part of:

  • Basic Structure.

83. Purpose of Judicial Review

Judicial Review:

  • Protects Constitution.
  • Safeguards Fundamental Rights.
  • Prevents arbitrary power.
  • Maintains constitutional supremacy.
  • Preserves democratic governance.

84. Separation of Powers

Governmental powers are distributed among:

  • Legislature.
  • Executive.
  • Judiciary.

85. Indian Position

India does not follow:

  • Rigid Separation of Powers.

Instead, it follows:

  • Functional Separation.
  • Checks and Balances.

  • Follow prescribed procedures.

96. Limits on Administrative Discretion

Administrative discretion:

Must remain within:

  • Constitutional authority.
  • Statutory limits.
  • Public purpose.

97. Accountability

Rule of Law ensures:

  • Officials remain subject to law.
  • Government decisions may be reviewed.
  • Illegal action may be challenged.
  • Abuse of power can attract legal consequences.

98. Transparency

Transparent Government action should be:

  • Open.
  • Fair.
  • Reasoned.
  • Consistent with law.

99. Constitutional Governance

Constitutional Governance means every organ of Government functions:

  • Within constitutional limits.
  • According to law.
  • Subject to Judicial Review where applicable.

100. Limited Constitutional Exceptions

Equality Before Law is not absolute.

The source identifies lawful exceptions such as:

  • President and Governor immunities.
  • Parliamentary privileges.
  • Judicial immunity.
  • Diplomatic immunity.
  • Reasonable classification.
  • Protective discrimination.
  • Martial law provisions.
  • Emergency provisions.

101. Article 361 — President

During tenure, President enjoys specified constitutional immunities.

These include:

  • Not answerable to court for official exercise of powers and duties.
  • No criminal proceedings instituted or continued.
  • No arrest or imprisonment.
  • Personal civil proceedings subject to prescribed notice.

102. Article 361 — Governor

Governor enjoys similar constitutional immunities during tenure regarding:

  • Official acts.
  • Criminal proceedings.
  • Arrest.
  • Personal civil proceedings subject to prescribed notice.

Article 361 → President + Governor Immunities

108. Article 34

Article 34 concerns:

  • Restrictions on Fundamental Rights while Martial Law is in force in an area.
  • Parliamentary indemnity for specified acts under constitutional conditions.

109. Emergency Powers

During National Emergency:

  • Certain Fundamental Rights may be affected according to constitutional provisions.

Emergency powers remain governed by:

  • Constitution.
  • Judicial Review where applicable.

110. Why Exceptions Do Not Destroy Rule of Law

These exceptions remain consistent with Rule of Law because they are:

  • Authorised by Constitution or law.
  • Created for legitimate purposes.
  • Limited by constitutional conditions.
  • Not based merely on arbitrary privilege.

Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected

What is Rule of Law? → Supremacy of law and subjection of every person and authority to law.

Who is associated with the modern exposition of Rule of Law? → A.V. Dicey.

Which book did Dicey write? → Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution.

Which year is associated with it? → 1885.

What are Dicey's three principles? → Supremacy of Law, Equality Before Law and Predominance of Legal Spirit.

What does Supremacy of Law mean? → No arbitrary Government power and no punishment except according to law.

What does Equality Before Law mean? → Ordinary citizens and public officials are equally subject to law.

What does Predominance of Legal Spirit mean? → Rights are protected through independent courts and legal remedies.

Does the Constitution expressly define “Rule of Law” in one Article? → No.

Is Rule of Law part of Basic Structure according to the attachment? → Yes.

Which Article is the strongest direct constitutional expression of equality? → Article 14.

What two expressions appear in Article 14? → Equality Before Law and Equal Protection of Laws.

What is the origin of Equality Before Law? → British Rule of Law.

What is its nature? → Negative concept.

What is the origin of Equal Protection of Laws? → U.S. Constitution.

What is its nature? → Positive concept.

Does Article 14 prohibit all classification? → No.

What does it prohibit? → Arbitrary classification.

What are the two tests of reasonable classification? → Intelligible Differentia and Rational Nexus.

Does Article 14 prohibit arbitrary State action? → Yes.

Which case is especially associated with arbitrariness under Article 14? → E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu, 1974.

Which Article prohibits specified discrimination? → Article 15.

Which Article guarantees equality in public employment? → Article 16.

Which Article abolishes untouchability? → Article 17.

Which Article abolishes titles subject to military and academic exceptions? → Article 18.

Which Article protects six major freedoms stated in the source? → Article 19.

Which Article provides criminal-law safeguards? → Article 20.

What are the three major safeguards under Article 20? → Ex post facto laws, double jeopardy and self-incrimination.

Which Article protects life and personal liberty? → Article 21.

What phrase is used in Article 21? → Procedure Established by Law.

Which case held the procedure must be fair, just and reasonable? → Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, 1978.

Which Article provides Right to Education? → Article 21A.

What age group? → 6–14 years.

Which Article contains safeguards against arrest and detention? → Article 22.

Which Article provides Right to Constitutional Remedies? → Article 32.

Who called Article 32 Heart and Soul of Constitution? → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.

Which Article gives High Courts wider writ jurisdiction? → Article 226.

Why is Article 226 wider? → It covers Fundamental Rights and other legal rights.

Which Article deals with equal justice and free legal aid? → Article 39A.

Which Article directs separation of Judiciary from Executive? → Article 50.

Which Article provides Special Leave to Appeal? → Article 136.

Which Article makes Supreme Court law binding? → Article 141.

Which Article provides Complete Justice? → Article 142.

Which Article gives High Courts superintendence? → Article 227.

Which Article protects property from deprivation without authority of law? → Article 300A.

Is Right to Property a Fundamental Right? → No.

What is it now? → Constitutional Right.

Which Article provides immunities to President and Governors? → Article 361.

Can criminal proceedings be instituted or continued against President or Governor during tenure under Article 361? → No.

Can they be arrested or imprisoned during tenure? → No.

Which Article deals with Parliament's privileges? → Article 105.

Which Article deals with State Legislature privileges? → Article 194.

Which Convention is associated with diplomatic immunity? → Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, 1961.

What is Natural Justice? → Fundamental fairness in decision-making.

What are its two major principles? → Nemo Judex in Causa Sua and Audi Alteram Partem.

What does Nemo Judex mean? → No one should be judge in own cause.

What is it called? → Rule Against Bias.

What does Audi Alteram Partem mean? → Hear the Other Side.

What does it ensure? → Notice and fair opportunity to be heard.

What is Administrative Fairness? → Administration according to law, reason, fairness and non-arbitrariness.

What is Judicial Review? → Examination of constitutional validity of laws and executive actions.

Is Judicial Review part of Basic Structure? → Yes.

Does India follow rigid Separation of Powers? → No.

What system does India follow? → Functional Separation with Checks and Balances.

What is Good Governance? → Transparent, accountable, responsive, efficient, equitable, participatory and lawful administration.

Does Rule of Law prohibit all constitutional exceptions to equality? → No.

Why are lawful exceptions valid? → They are constitutionally or legally authorised for legitimate purposes.

Which Article deals with Martial Law-related constitutional protection? → Article 34.

Which Amendment is called Mini Constitution? → 42nd Amendment, 1976.

What did 42nd Amendment add to Preamble? → Socialist, Secular and Integrity.

Which Amendment restored several judicial powers curtailed by 42nd Amendment? → 43rd Amendment, 1977.

Which Amendment restored democratic safeguards and created Article 300A framework? → 44th Amendment, 1978.

Which Amendment reduced voting age to 18? → 61st Amendment, 1988.

Which Amendment constitutionalised Panchayats? → 73rd Amendment.

Which Amendment constitutionalised Municipalities? → 74th Amendment.

Which Amendment inserted Article 21A? → 86th Amendment, 2002.

Which Amendment inserted Articles 15(6) and 16(6)? → 103rd Amendment, 2019.

What did the 103rd Amendment provide? → 10% EWS reservation.

Which case upheld 103rd Amendment according to the attachment? → Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India, 2022.

Which case evolved Basic Structure Doctrine? → Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, 1973.

Which case held arbitrariness is antithetical to equality? → E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu, 1974.

Which case associated Rule of Law with democratic election principles? → Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain, 1975.

Which controversial Emergency case concerned personal liberty? → A.D.M. Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla, 1976.

Which later case expressly rejected the constitutional approach taken in A.D.M. Jabalpur according to the attachment? → K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India, 2017.

Which case expanded Article 21? → Maneka Gandhi, 1978.

Which case established Judicial Review and limited amending power as Basic Structure features? → Minerva Mills, 1980.

Which case strengthened administrative non-arbitrariness under Article 14? → Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib Sehravardi, 1981.

Which case held post-24 April 1973 Ninth Schedule laws are reviewable if they damage Basic Structure? → I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu, 2007.

Which case recognised Right to Privacy? → K.S. Puttaswamy, 2017.

Which case reinforced equality, dignity, privacy and personal liberty in relation to consensual same-sex relations? → Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India, 2018.

What is the easiest Rule-of-Law memory line? → Dicey: Supremacy of Law + Equality Before Law + Predominance of Legal Spirit; Constitution: Article 14 + Article 21 + Judicial Review + Independent Judiciary.
